title: Today State Share: How Are You Feeling Today?
lead: Everyone has a different kind of day, and that's worth sharing. Pick the state that best matches your today, from bright and buzzing to calm, tired, or somewhere in between. Browse the groups, find your vibe, and share it with friends.

items.name: Rio Carnival (Carnaval do Rio de Janeiro)
items.text: A huge festival held before Lent in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Many visitors are surprised that samba schools spend almost a full year preparing costumes and floats. Locals enjoy street parties called blocos and the Sambadrome parades.

items.name: Daruma doll (達磨)
items.text: A round, red Japanese doll that represents perseverance. It usually comes with both eyes blank. People paint in one eye when they set a goal and the second eye once they reach it, often at New Year.

items.name: Holi (होली)
items.text: A Hindu spring festival celebrated mainly in India and Nepal. It marks the victory of good over evil and the arrival of spring. People throw colored powder and water at friends, family and even strangers, then share sweets.

items.name: Radio Taiso (ラジオ体操)
items.text: A short set of calisthenics set to piano music and broadcast on Japanese radio since 1928. It surprises people how widely it is practiced. Schools, workplaces and neighborhood groups do it together, especially on summer mornings.

items.name: Aurora (Northern Lights)
items.text: Glowing curtains of green, pink and violet light. They appear when charged particles from the Sun hit Earth's upper atmosphere. In places like Norway, Finland, Iceland and Canada, people head out on dark winter nights to watch them dance overhead.

items.name: Haka
items.text: A traditional Māori ceremonial dance from New Zealand, performed with strong chanting, stamping and fierce facial expressions. Many people know it only from rugby matches. In fact, it is also performed at weddings, funerals and to honor guests.

items.name: La Tomatina
items.text: A festival in Buñol, Spain, held on the last Wednesday of August, where participants throw ripe tomatoes at each other in the streets. Afterward, the streets are hosed down, and the tomato acidity is said to leave them notably clean.

items.name: Labor Thanksgiving Day (勤労感謝の日)
items.text: A Japanese national holiday on November 23 for honoring work and thanking one another. It has roots in Niiname-sai, an ancient harvest festival. Children often make cards or drawings to thank family members and local workers.

items.name: Hot spring bathing (Onsen)
items.text: Japan's natural hot springs, heated by volcanic activity, are found across the country. Visitors are often surprised that bathers wash thoroughly before entering and soak without swimsuits. Locals enjoy long, quiet soaks, often followed by a light meal or a nap.

items.name: Japanese rock garden (Karesansui)
items.text: A dry landscape garden of raked gravel, stones and moss, often found at Zen temples such as Ryōan-ji in Kyoto. Many are surprised that the gravel patterns represent water. People sit on temple verandas and quietly contemplate the scene.

items.name: Fika (Swedish coffee break)
items.text: Fika is the Swedish custom of pausing for coffee, often with a cinnamon bun or pastry, together with friends or colleagues. Visitors are surprised that many workplaces build it into the day. Swedes treat it as a moment to slow down and connect.

items.name: Japanese calligraphy (Shodō)
items.text: Shodō is the art of writing characters with brush and ink. People are often surprised that each stroke follows a set order and cannot be corrected once made. Many Japanese practice it at school, and New Year's kakizome is a cherished tradition.

items.name: Lagom
items.text: Lagom is a Swedish word meaning "just the right amount" — not too much, not too little. Many are surprised there is no exact English equivalent. Swedes apply it to everyday life, from work-life balance to sharing food and resources fairly.

items.name: Hygge
items.text: Hygge is a Danish and Norwegian idea of cozy contentment and warm togetherness. Visitors are surprised how central candles are; Denmark is known for high candle use. Locals enjoy it with friends, warm drinks, soft lighting and relaxed conversation during long winters.

items.name: Japanese tea ceremony (Sadō / Chadō)
items.text: The tea ceremony is a ritual preparation and serving of matcha, shaped by Zen ideas and the tea master Sen no Rikyū. Guests are often surprised how every gesture, from bowing to turning the bowl, carries meaning. Practitioners value calm attention and respect.

items.name: Onsen (温泉)
items.text: Onsen are Japan's natural hot springs, heated by volcanic activity. Visitors are often surprised that people bathe without swimwear, after washing thoroughly first. Locals soak slowly, then relax in a yukata with a meal at a traditional inn.

items.name: Siesta (siesta)
items.text: A siesta is a short rest or nap after the midday meal, traditionally linked with Spain. Many visitors are surprised that some shops still close in the early afternoon. Locals use these quiet hours for a long lunch and rest.

items.name: Finnish Sauna (sauna)
items.text: The sauna is a hot room for sweat bathing and a central part of Finnish life. People are often surprised that Finland has millions of saunas. Finns alternate the heat with cooling off, sometimes by jumping into a lake.

items.name: Kotatsu (炬燵)
items.text: A kotatsu is a low Japanese table covered by a heavy blanket, with a heater underneath. Many people are surprised how hard it is to leave once seated. Families gather around it in winter to eat mandarin oranges and chat.

items.name: Forest Bathing (森林浴, shinrin-yoku)
items.text: Forest bathing is a practice named in Japan in the 1980s: spending slow, mindful time among trees using all five senses. People are surprised it has no hiking goal at all. Locals stroll, breathe deeply and simply rest.

items.name: Espresso (caffè espresso)
items.text: Espresso is a small, strong Italian coffee made by forcing hot water through finely ground beans. Visitors are often surprised that many Italians drink it quickly while standing at the bar. Locals simply order "un caffè" throughout the day.

items.name: Hygge (hygge)
items.text: Hygge is a Danish word for a cozy, contented mood. People are often surprised it has no exact English translation. Danes create it with candles, warm drinks, soft blankets and unhurried time with friends, especially during long, dark winters.

items.name: Anxiety (不安, Fuan)
items.text: Anxiety is a feeling of worry or unease about something that might happen. Many people are surprised that it is a normal protective response. Slow breathing, a short walk, or talking with a trusted friend often helps it ease.

items.name: Stress (ストレス, Sutoresu)
items.text: Stress is the body and mind reacting to pressure from work, school, or daily life. Surprisingly, short bursts can sharpen focus. Many people unwind with rest, light exercise, warm baths, or simply sharing how their day went.

items.name: Feeling Overwhelmed
items.text: Feeling overwhelmed happens when tasks, emotions, or information pile up faster than you can handle them. It often feels bigger than it is. Writing a short list, picking one small step, and pausing for a break can restore calm.

items.name: Confusion (混乱, Konran)
items.text: Confusion is the sense of not quite understanding a situation or what to do next. It is often a sign that learning is happening. Asking questions, slowing down, and revisiting things after rest usually brings clarity.

items.name: Restlessness
items.text: Restlessness is an uneasy inability to sit still or settle down, felt in both body and mind. It can come from excess energy, boredom, or worry. Stretching, moving around, or changing scenery often helps people feel settled again.

items.name: Distraction
items.text: Distraction is when attention keeps drifting away from what you want to focus on. Phones and notifications are common causes, but tiredness plays a part too. Many people try short focused sessions, quiet spaces, or simply putting devices aside.

items.name: Nervousness (緊張, Kinchō)
items.text: Nervousness is the jittery feeling before something important, like a test, speech, or first meeting. A racing heart or butterflies in the stomach are common. Deep breaths, preparation, and reminding yourself it shows you care can help.

items.name: Hygge (Danish)
items.text: Hygge is the Danish idea of cozy contentment found in simple moments. Many are surprised it describes a mood rather than a thing. Danes enjoy it with candles, warm drinks, soft blankets and unhurried time with friends during long winters.

items.name: Fado (Portuguese music)
items.text: Fado is a Portuguese song tradition known for its sorrowful, deeply emotional melodies. It is listed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. In Lisbon and Coimbra, people listen quietly in small taverns, where singers perform with Portuguese guitar accompaniment.

items.name: Nighthawks (Edward Hopper painting)
items.text: Nighthawks is Edward Hopper's 1942 painting of a few people in a late-night diner seen through a large glass window. Many people find it captures urban loneliness. Visitors view it at the Art Institute of Chicago.

items.name: Valentine's Day in Japan (バレンタインデー)
items.text: In Japan, Valentine's Day is traditionally when people give chocolate to loved ones, friends and coworkers. Many visitors are surprised that a return-gift day, White Day, follows a month later on March 14.

items.name: Saudade (Portuguese)
items.text: Saudade is a Portuguese and Brazilian word for a deep, longing nostalgia for someone or something absent. It is often called hard to translate. People express it through songs, poetry and conversations about distant places and loved ones.

items.name: Senbazuru (千羽鶴)
items.text: Senbazuru is a string of one thousand folded origami cranes, traditionally linked with wishes for recovery and peace. Through the story of Sadako Sasaki, it became a symbol of hope. People fold them together for the sick or for peace memorials.

items.name: Hachikō (ハチ公)
items.text: Hachikō was an Akita dog who waited at Tokyo's Shibuya Station for his owner for years after the owner's death. His loyalty moves people worldwide. His bronze statue outside the station is a famous meeting spot today.

items.name: Pomodoro Technique
items.text: A time management method created by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s. You work in focused 25-minute blocks separated by short breaks. It is named after his tomato-shaped kitchen timer, and people worldwide use apps or simple timers to follow it.

items.name: Getting Things Done (GTD)
items.text: A productivity method described by David Allen in his 2001 book. Its core idea is to move every task out of your head into a trusted system. Busy people review their lists weekly to regain control when work piles up.

items.name: Human multitasking
items.text: Doing several tasks at once, or switching quickly between them. Research shows the brain usually switches attention rather than truly working in parallel, and each switch can cost time and accuracy. Many people batch similar tasks to reduce switching.

items.name: Parkinson's law
items.text: The observation that "work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion." British historian C. Northcote Parkinson wrote it in a 1955 essay in The Economist. Many people set shorter self-imposed deadlines to stay on track.

items.name: Flow (psychology)
items.text: A state of deep, energized focus in which time seems to disappear. Psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi named and studied it. It tends to appear when a task's challenge matches your skill, and athletes, musicians and programmers alike seek it out.

items.name: Planning fallacy
items.text: The tendency to underestimate how long a task will take, even with past experience of overruns. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky proposed the idea in 1979. Adding buffer time and checking how long similar tasks took before can help.

items.name: Ramen (ラーメン)
items.text: Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup with wheat noodles in a rich broth, often flavored with soy sauce, miso, salt or pork bone. Many people are surprised by how much it varies by region. Locals slurp it hot, and slurping is perfectly polite.

items.name: Cabinet of Curiosities (Wunderkammer)
items.text: A cabinet of curiosities was a room or cabinet in Renaissance Europe filled with fossils, shells, art and strange objects. People are often surprised that these private collections helped shape the first modern museums. Today they inspire exhibitions and home displays.

items.name: Kendama (けん玉)
items.text: Kendama is a traditional Japanese skill toy: a wooden handle with cups and a spike, attached by string to a ball. It looks simple, but there are thousands of tricks. Players of all ages practice for fun, and some compete in tournaments.

items.name: Limerick
items.text: A limerick is a short, playful poem of five lines with an AABBA rhyme scheme and a bouncy rhythm. Many people are surprised that Edward Lear made the form famous in the 1800s. Friends trade them for laughs and often invent their own.

items.name: Camino de Santiago (Way of St. James)
items.text: The Camino de Santiago is a network of pilgrimage routes leading to the cathedral in Santiago de Compostela, Spain. People are often surprised that walkers of every faith and none take part. Pilgrims carry a credential stamped at hostels along the way.

items.name: Japanese Rock Garden (枯山水, karesansui)
items.text: A Japanese rock garden uses stones, moss and raked gravel to suggest water, mountains and islands without any actual water. Visitors are often surprised how calming the empty space feels. People sit quietly on temple verandas, letting their minds wander.

items.name: Rice Porridge (お粥, okayu)
items.text: Rice porridge, known as congee in much of Asia and okayu in Japan, is rice simmered in plenty of water until soft. Many are surprised how many cultures serve it to people feeling unwell. It is often topped with pickled plum or ginger.
